The open-source LLM ecosystem could really benefit from an LLM building-block API. We have so many LLM components across different models now. Whether you are using PyTorch or C++ and CUDA code directly, there is a major switching cost when you want to run experiments or ablation studies, say swapping GQA with MLA, dense FFNs with MoE, attention layers with Mamba2 or Gated DeltaNet, or standard residual connections with attention residuals. Currently, it’s very messy even with LLM-assisted coding. It could maybe be on top of PyTorch or CUDA directly, but it needs to be carefully engineered and maintained (versus quickly vibe-coded on a weekend) and efficient enough that people trust it to use in production (which is really a requirement to move beyond toy examples). Maybe some food for thought for a big, well-funded lab :) (There are some efforts that go into that direction, like torchtitan, torchtune, Megatron Core, OLMo-core, but they are not quite that level of abstraction, I'd say. And, as always, there’s the chicken-and-egg problem: it needs to be popular to get widely adopted, and it needs to get widely adopted to become popular.)

Self-improving AI is one of the most discussed ideas right now. This is one of the most exciting papers I've read recently on the topic. (bookmark it) It proposes AutoRL, which lifts Qwen3 on AIME 2024 from 46.67% to 66.67% by letting agents supervise a live RL run instead of following a fixed recipe. AutoRL works like an RL researcher on call. Perceptor agents watch training curves, rollouts, and evaluations and flag problems. Three Proposer agents diagnose the issue and suggest changes. An Orchestrator approves them and applies them with a hot update or a restart from a checkpoint. On math, AIME 2025 and HMMT 2025 each improve by 11.67 points. On agentic coding with LongCat-Flash-Lite, pass@1 rises from 52.29% to 65.13% over a long unattended run with interruptions. Given a deliberately broken recipe, AutoRL found and fixed the problems. The authors say agents can already handle routine RL supervision. Validating each change still takes a lot of compute. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17790 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/autorl-a-multi-agent-system-towards-autonomous-reinforcement-learning-2611.17790

Great practical paper on speeding up agent evals and RL rollouts. For agent batches, they suggest running the longest trajectories first, because they determine when the whole batch finishes. Agent tasks alternate between model inference and environment steps, so GPUs and sandboxes wait on each other. The Ling team schedules both together. Trajectories stay on the workers that hold their KV cache, and when environment slots are limited, the longest chains get priority. On BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas, batch completion time drops by 10.4% to 65.0% with the same evaluation scores. The methods now run in training and evaluation for the Ling-3.x models. Takeaway: If your eval runs end with a few long trajectories while the other workers sit idle, look at scheduling before buying more GPUs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16661 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/reducing-batch-makespan-for-llm-agent-workloads-through-inference-environment-co-2611.16661

What was the significance of this weekend's SpaceX tower catch: "Catching the second stage is substantially harder than catching the first stage because the Ship returns from orbit while the booster returns from a short suborbital hop. The booster separates minutes after liftoff, performs a brief boostback, and comes back from only a few hundred kilometers away at relatively low speed. Ship must reach orbital velocity, deploy payload, coast for many hours, execute a precise deorbit burn, survive full reentry heating, and only then perform its landing burn. As such, Ship must carry a functional heat shield, fly a long guided atmospheric trajectory from the other side of the planet, and execute a high-energy flip into the “chopsticks” while protecting its heat-shield side. Those combined demands of orbital energy, thermal protection, long-range guidance, and final precision are why a Ship catch is so incredibly difficult. No prior system, including the Space Shuttle, recovered a rocket-style orbital stage in this manner. The catch validates the path to full reusability which is the foundation of Starship’s cost and cadence targets. This is particularly important in driving the economics of orbital data centers." - DB

Super interesting work from Microsoft and colleagues. They take a closer look at the exciting research area of weight-space programming. They had Claude Opus 5.5 write transformer weights directly in code, with no gradient training. The smallest models that solved the algorithmic tasks had a median of 166 parameters. The method is called interpretable weight-space programming. An agent proposes a computation, writes it as explicit weights and features, tests it, and revises it for 30 to 50 rounds. A person can read the result line by line. All 26 runs on algorithmic tasks reached 100% accuracy on held-out data, often by writing a known algorithm into the weights. They find that the model matters. Sonnet 5.5 needed a median of 41,600 parameters, and Haiku 5.5 needed 100,000. Language tasks were harder. Those models stayed near 190,000 parameters and lost accuracy against learned baselines. They then used the same loop on brain data. In the visual cortex, it predicted responses better than existing interpretable models. In language fMRI, it found a confound in the dataset. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18114 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/interpretable-weight-space-programming-builds-transparent-transformers-and-brain-2611.18114
